To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Mg-Zr biodegradable alloys with appropriate quantities of calcium or strontium are efficient in inducing good-quality osseointegration.
Mg-Zr based biodegradable implants containing appropriate quantities of calcium and strontium could be very effective for inducing bone formation.
strontium and calcium containing Mg-Zr alloys have been shown to be effective in promoting osseointegration.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of novel biodegradable orthopaedic devices and the associated biological properties of such devices.
developing new biodegradable alloys that are capable of mimicking the physicochemical and biologic properties of bone, and thus can be used as orthopedic implants.
developing novel biodegradable implant materials, which are capable of inducing good quality bone tissue at the site of implantation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

strontium and calcium containing Mg-Zr alloys can be considered as potential candidates for orthopedic implants, and further studies are warranted to optimize their compositions for specific orthopedic applications.
the Mg-Zr alloys with appropriate quantity of strontium are more suitable for inducing good quality bone than other alloys.
Mg-Zr based alloys with strontium could be a potential candidate for orthopedic implants.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the biodegradability of Mg-Zr implants can be modulated by the incorporation of strontium and/or calcium, and the resultant biodegradability would depend on the quantity of these alloying elements in the alloys.
strontium containing magnesium-zirconium alloys are promising biodegradable materials for orthopedic applications.

strontium is more effective than calcium in inducing bone-like properties in Mg-Zr alloys, and that strontium and calcium are effective in inducing bone-like tissue when they are present in the alloy at appropriate concentrations.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the biodegradable implants should not be treated as inert objects, but they should be treated as active components that can modulate the biological processes.
the addition of calcium and strontium to magnesium based biodegradables could be used to control the rate of bone formation.

Mg-Zr alloy containing 1% Sr was the most efficient in inducing bone formation, while the other three alloys containing different quantities (1, 3, and 5% Ca) of calcium were relatively less effective in inducing bone formation.
